images.title: Alforjas magnifontis
images.description: This camel was originally described as a species of Pliauchenia .

images.title: Barbourofelis loveorum
images.description: This false saber-tooth cat was the size of a lion. The species B. loveorum has been found in Late Miocene layers of North America from Florida to California.

images.title: Woodburnehyus grenaderae
images.description: This ancient peccary found at the Blackhawk Ranch quarry at the foot of Mount Diablo, in California, sported some bizarre protrusions on the cheeks (they were however less pronounced than in the related genus Skinnerhyus ).

images.title: Ustatochoerus major
images.description: This oreodont (a group of completely extinct even-toed ungulates) was originally described as a species of the genus Merychyus . Fossils of this animal have been found in Late Miocene layers at several places in North America from California to Texas.

images.title: Epicyon diabloensis
images.description: This small species of "bone crushing" dog has been discovered in the famous Black Hawk Ranch fossil quarry on the south side of Mount Diablo. Originally described as "Osteoborus diabloensis" in 1938, it was later reclassified as belonging to the genus Epicyon .

images.title: Diadiaphorus majusculus
images.description: Meridiungulates are a group of diverse extinct ungulates restricted to South America. They were driven to extinction after the Great American Interchange which occurred when North and South America get connected through the isthmus of Panama, out-competed by the North American ungulates.

images.title: Theosodon garretorum
images.description: Litopterns form one of the groups of peculiar hoofed mammals (ungulates) that evolved in isolation in South America. Mitochondrial DNA analysis of a fossil litoptern indicated that they were closely related to the odd-toed ungulates (Perissodactyla: horses, tapirs and rhinos).

images.title: Menura tyawanoides
images.description: This bird is known from a single bone showing that it was a lyrebird. It was smaller than its modern counterpart.

images.title: Sthenurus stirlingi
images.description: Sthenurus stirlingi was a large short-faced kangaroo from the Pleistocene of Australia. Possessing a deep, robust skull adapted for chewing tough browse, forward-facing binocular vision, and single-toed hind feet with hooved claws, it engaged in upright bipedal striding rather than bounding like modern kangaroos.

images.title: Argyrolagus palmeri
images.description: Argyrolagus was a diminutive 40-cm bipedal saltatorial marsupial from the Pliocene of Argentina. Showcasing astonishing convergent evolution with modern kangaroo rats and jerboas, it possessed greatly elongated hind legs, a long balancing tail, reduced forelimbs, and large orbits indicating nocturnal foraging for desert seeds.

images.title: Euryzygoma dunense
images.description: Euryzygoma was an unusual 2.5-meter, half-tonne diprotodontid marsupial from the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene of Queensland, Australia. It was distinguished by extraordinarily flared, saucer-like cheekbone flanges (zygomatic arches) that likely anchored massive cheek pouches for storing browse or functioned in visual display and intraspecific combat.

images.title: Dusisiren jordani
images.description: Dusisiren jordani was a 4.3-meter, 3-to-4-tonne extinct dugongid sirenian from the Late Miocene to Pliocene of the North Pacific (California and Japan). Representing a transitional stage in the evolution of Steller's sea cow (Hydrodamalis), it possessed reduced front limb flippers and grazed on kelp beds in temperate coastal waters.

images.title: Eucladoceros dicranios
images.description: Height: 1.8 m The males of this large prehistoric deer from Europe developed extraordinary antlers which look a bit like those of the legendary Pokemon Xerneas. The genus seems to have originated in China where the earliest remains (Early Pliocene) have been found.

images.title: Kvabebihyrax kachethicus
images.description: Hyraxes are today only represented by four small herbivorous animals that lived in Africa and the Middle-East. Despite their superficially rodent-like aspect, hyraxes are actually more closely related to elephants and manatees.

images.title: Anancus arvernensis
images.description: Anancus was characterized by its extremely long tusks. The genus flourished from the Late Miocene to the Early Pleistocene and was represented by several species in Europe, Asia and Africa.

images.title: Toxodon platensis
images.description: Toxodon was a massive 2.7-meter, 1.5-tonne herbivorous notoungulate from the Late Pliocene to Late Pleistocene of South America. Featuring arched, chisel-like constantly growing incisors, high-crowned cheek teeth, and short graviportal legs, it was famously discovered by Charles Darwin during the Beagle voyage and described as one of the strangest animals ever discovered.

images.title: Semirostrum ceruttii
images.description: Semirostrum was an extraordinary 1.8-meter fossil porpoise from the Pliocene (Purisima and San Diego Formations) of California. It featured a bizarre elongated, toothless lower jaw symphysis resembling the bill of a modern skimmer bird, which it dragged through coastal muddy sediments to locate bottom-dwelling fish and invertebrates.

images.title: Megantereon cultridens
images.description: Megantereon was a slenderly built saber-toothed cat from Europe, Asia, Africa and North America. It was probably ancestral to Smilodon .

images.title: Dinopithecus ingens
images.description: Dinopithecus was a giant baboon as big as a man from the Pliocene of South Africa .

images.title: Nuralagus rex
images.description: Nuralagus ("Minorca hare") is the largest known rabbit, with an estimated weight of 12 kg. It lived during the Pliocene period, endemic to the island of Minorca.

images.title: Crocodylus anthropophagus
images.description: This large "horned" crocodile was the largest predator known to the early hominid Homo habilis . Despite what its specific name may indicate, there is no direct evidence that it exclusively fed on humans.

images.title: Homo erectus
images.description: Homo erectus ('upright man') was a highly successful, wide-ranging early human species that emerged in the Early Pleistocene (~1.9 Ma) in Africa and spread across Eurasia. Characterized by modern human-like body proportions, an enlarged brain (700-1100 cc), Acheulean bifacial handaxe technology, and the systematic use of controlled fire, it persisted until ~110,000 years ago.

images.title: Australopithecus afarensis
images.description: Australopithecus afarensis was an extinct gracile hominin that lived between ~3.9 and 2.9 Ma during the Pliocene of East Africa (famous from the 'Lucy' skeleton and Laetoli footprints). Combining obligate bipedal terrestrial locomotion with curved fingers and shoulders suited for arboreal climbing, it had an ape-like brain volume (~400-500 cc) and pronounced facial prognathism.

images.title: Ardipithecus ramidus
images.description: Ardipithecus ramidus ('Ardi') was an early hominin that lived around 4.4 Ma during the Early Pliocene in the Middle Awash of Ethiopia. Representing a pivotal stage near the human-chimpanzee divergence, it featured a grasping, opposable big toe for clambering in trees alongside a modified pelvis adapted for facultative bipedalism on the ground.

images.title: Acinonyx kurteni
images.description: Acinonyx kurteni (the 'Linxia cheetah') was described in 2008 as a primitive Late Pliocene cheetah from the Linxia Basin of Gansu, China. Later anatomical re-examinations revealed the holotype skull to be an elaborate composite forgery fabricated from plaster and fossil fragments, leading to the retraction of its cheetah status and serving as a cautionary tale in modern vertebrate paleontology.

images.title: Arctodus simus
images.description: The giant short-faced bear ( Arctodus simus ) was one of the largest land predator that ever existed. Neither a super-predator nor a strict scavenger, it was most probably an opportunistic omnivore like modern brown bears.

images.title: Miracinonyx trumani
images.description: The "American cheetah" was previously though to be closely related to the African cheetah and placed in the same genus Acinonyx . However, DNA analysis later indicated that its closest living relative is in fact the puma (also named cougar or mountain lion).

images.title: Homo longi
images.description: Dragon Man ( Homo longi ) is a recently discovered ancient human known from a nearly complete skull. Characterized a low, long and robust skull with a large nasal opening, it was adapted to the cold climates of the Pleistocene Ice Ages.

images.title: Procoptodon goliah
images.description: The genus Procoptodon ("forward hill tooth") includes the largest kangaroo that ever lived, P. goliah . This short-faced browser was too big to be able to hop and it was proposed that it walked on its two legs the way humans do.

images.title: Meleagris californica
images.description: Meleagris californica is an extinct species of turkey that lived in California to as late as 10,000 BC. It was one of the most common birds found trapped in the Rancho La Brea pit.

images.title: Dinornis robustus
images.description: The South Island giant moa (Dinornis robustus) was a colossal flightless ratite endemic to New Zealand, standing up to 3.6 meters tall with its neck outstretched and weighing up to 250 kg. Completely lacking wing bones, it was the tallest bird known to have lived, browsing subalpine forests until driven to extinction following human settlement in the 15th century.

images.title: Coelodonta antiquitatis
images.description: The woolly rhinoceros was well adapted to the cold climate of the ice age. Its aspect is known from frozen individuals found in Siberia as well as from numerous prehistoric cave paintings.

images.title: Megaloceros giganteus
images.description: Megaloceros giganteus (the Irish elk or giant deer) was an immense cervid standing over 2.1 meters at the shoulder that ranged across Eurasia during the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene. Mature stags grew the largest antlers of any known deer, spanning up to 3.65 meters and weighing up to 40 kg, adapted for acoustic resonance and intimidating rivals during the autumn rut.

images.title: Elasmotherium sibiricum
images.description: This Eurasian rhinoceros had a single horn on the top of its head. The exact shape of the horn is speculative as it has not been preserved by fossilization.

images.title: Nothrotheriops shastensis
images.description: The Shasta Ground Sloth is the most common Ground Slot found in the La Brea Tar Pits in California, and remains of this animal have been found throughout the South Western part of the United States. Preserved dried dungs found in caves of this animal indicate that it played an important role on the dispersal of the Joshua Trees.

images.title: Camelops hesternus
images.description: Camelops hesternus ('yesterday's camel') was a 2.2-meter tall, 800-kg true camelid that roamed open plains, grasslands, and deserts of western North America during the Pleistocene. Possessing a single dorsal adipose hump like modern dromedaries and specialized foot pads for desert and prairie travel, it survived until the end-Pleistocene megafaunal extinction ~11,000 years ago.

images.title: Megatherium americanum
images.description: As big as an elephant, Megatherium is the largest known ground sloth. It was normally quadrupedal but was able to stand on its hind legs.

images.title: Mammut americanum
images.description: The American mastodon (Mammut americanum) was a heavily built, 3-meter tall proboscidean that inhabited spruce woodlands and wetlands across North America during the Pleistocene. Characterized by long, curved upper tusks and high-crested zygodont molar crowns adapted for browsing woody twigs and conifers, it vanished at the close of the Pleistocene around 10,000 years ago.

images.title: Mammuthus columbi
images.description: The Columbia Mammoth was one of the last large animal (megafauna) of North America. It was closely related to the Woolly Mammoth but lived in warmer climate.

images.title: Mammuthus meridionalis
images.description: Mammuthus meridionalis (the southern mammoth) was a colossal early mammoth standing 4 meters tall and weighing up to 10 to 11 tonnes that roamed open woodlands of Europe and Central Asia during the Early Pleistocene (~2.5-1.5 Ma). Adapted to milder, temperate climates before the onset of intense ice ages, it possessed robust spiraling tusks and was ancestral to steppe and woolly mammoths.

images.title: Blackhawk Ranch Fauna (Late Miocene California)
images.description: A composite reconstruction of the Late Miocene (Clarendonian, ~10-9 Ma) terrestrial mammal fauna from the Blackhawk Ranch quarry on Mount Diablo, California. Featured taxa include the camel Alforjas magnifontis, the bone-crushing dog Borophagus littoralis, the false saber-tooth cat Barbourofelis loveorum, the peccary Woodburnehyus grenaderae, the oreodont Ustatochoerus major, the three-toed horse Hipparion forcei, and the mastodont Gomphotherium obscurum.

images.title: Purisima Formation Marine Mammal Fauna
images.description: A composite reconstruction of the diverse coastal marine mammal fauna of the Upper Miocene to Pliocene (~7-3 Ma) Purisima Formation at Half Moon Bay, California. Featured species include the dwarf rorqual Balaenoptera bertae, the bizarre down-pointing tusked porpoise Semirostrum ceruttii, the double-tusked walrus Dusignathus santacruzensis, the northern fur seal Callorhinus gilmorei, the long-beaked dolphin Parapontoporia sternbergi, and the pygmy whale Herpetocetus bramblei.

images.title: Olenelloides armatus
images.description: Olenelloides armatus was an early trilobite from the Cambrian period, characterized by its segmented exoskeleton and prominent spines along its body. This small arthropod was an early marine predator and scavenger that inhabited ancient seafloors during the Cambrian explosion of life.

images.title: Wladysagitta janvieri
images.description: Wladysagitta janvieri is an early agnathan (jawless fish) from the Paleozoic Era, representing an ancient lineage of primitive vertebrates that lacked jaws and paired fins. These small, eel-like creatures were among the earliest vertebrates to evolve and diversified throughout ancient marine environments.

images.title: Leptauchenia decora
images.description: Leptauchenia decora was a small, rabbit-sized artiodactyl from the Oligocene epoch, belonging to the oreodont family. These herbivorous mammals were characterized by their slender limbs and delicate build, adapting to the arid grasslands and shrublands of North America.

images.title: Ernietta plateauensis
images.description: Ernietta plateauensis is a quilted, disc-shaped organism from the Ediacaran period, characterized by its segmented, ranged body plan that remains enigmatic in terms of its exact biological classification. This early complex life form represents one of the first macroscopic creatures to inhabit ancient seafloors before the Cambrian explosion.

images.title: Cloudina hartmannae
images.description: Cloudina hartmannae is an early skeletal organism from the Ediacaran period, characterized by conical, nested shells that formed a tubular structure. This diminutive creature represents one of the earliest examples of biomineralization and was likely a sessile filter-feeder inhabiting shallow marine environments.

images.title: Death Valley National Park Armored Jawless Fish
images.description: Armored jawless fish, or ostracoderms, were among the earliest vertebrates to develop protective bony plating covering their heads and bodies. These agnathans dominated early aquatic ecosystems before the evolution of jawed fish, representing a crucial stage in vertebrate armor evolution.

images.title: Obamus coronatus
images.description: Obamus coronatus is an extinct trilobite from the Ordovician period, characterized by its distinctive crowned or elaborate cephalon (head shield). This marine arthropod was a bottom-dwelling predator or scavenger that inhabited shallow Paleozoic seas.

images.title: Riograndia guaibensis
images.description: Riograndia guaibensis was a small, carnivorous therapsid from the Early Triassic of Brazil, representing one of the early synapsids that survived the Permian-Triassic extinction event. This early mammal-like reptile occupied ecological niches in the recovery ecosystems following the most severe mass extinction in Earth's history.

images.title: Macrocollum itaquii
images.description: Macrocollum itaquii is an early sauropodomorph from the Late Triassic of Brazil, representing a transitional form between basal sauropodomorphs and true sauropods. This long-necked herbivore demonstrates the early evolution of the gigantism and specialized feeding strategies that would characterize later sauropods.

images.title: Bagualosaurus agudoensis
images.description: Bagualosaurus agudoensis is an early sauropodomorph from the Late Triassic of Argentina, representing a transitional form between basal sauropodomorphs and later sauropods. This relatively small dinosaur exhibits characteristics that help illuminate the evolutionary pathway toward the giant herbivorous sauropods of the Mesozoic.

images.title: Lisowicia bojani
images.description: Lisowicia bojani was a large dicynodont therapsid from the Late Triassic of Poland, representing one of the largest synapsids of its time. This herbivorous mammal-like reptile possessed a stocky body plan and was well-adapted to the arid terrestrial environments of the Triassic period.

images.title: Mixosaurus cornalianus
images.description: Mixosaurus cornalianus was a small to medium-sized ichthyosaur from the Triassic period, characterized by a streamlined body adapted for efficient aquatic locomotion. As an early member of the ichthyosaur lineage, it represents an important transitional form in the evolution of these marine reptiles.

images.title: Laosuchus naga
images.description: Laosuchus naga is an early reptiliomorph from the Carboniferous period of Southeast Asia, representing an important transitional form in the evolution of amniotes. This small, lizard-like creature demonstrates the early adaptations that would eventually lead to the radiation of true reptiles.

images.title: Basal Ichthyopterygians
images.description: Basal ichthyopterygians represent the earliest and most primitive members of Ichthyosauria, a diverse group of marine reptiles that dominated ocean ecosystems from the Triassic through the Cretaceous. These early forms show transitional characteristics between their terrestrial ancestors and the highly specialized aquatic ichthyosaurs that would later evolve.

images.title: Trossingen Formation
images.description: The Trossingen Formation is a Late Triassic fossil site in Germany famous for its exceptional preservation of plateosaur remains and other early dinosaurs. This ecosystem represents an important window into the early evolution of dinosaurs during the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic period.

images.title: Staurikosaurus pricei
images.description: Staurikosaurus pricei was an early theropod dinosaur from the Middle Triassic of Brazil, representing one of the oldest known members of Herrerasauria. This small carnivore possessed the basic bipedal body plan and hunting adaptations that characterized early dinosauriform predators.

images.title: Ischigualasto Formation
images.description: The Ischigualasto Formation is a Late Triassic ecosystem from northwestern Argentina (approximately 231-228 million years ago) that preserves one of the earliest known dinosaur faunas. This fossil assemblage includes early dinosaurs such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus alongside non-dinosaurian reptiles, cynodonts, and other Triassic fauna, providing crucial insights into the early evolution and diversification of dinosaurs.

images.title: Early Deuterostomes
images.description: Early deuterostomes represent some of the earliest members of the group that would eventually give rise to echinoderms, hemichordates, and chordates. These organisms from the Cambrian period display the foundational body plans and developmental characteristics that distinguish deuterostomes from other animal groups.

images.title: Yunnanolepis chii
images.description: Yunnanolepis chii is an early placoderm fish from the Silurian period, characterized by its bony plated armor and primitive jawed structure. This small fish represents an important transitional form in the evolution of early vertebrates with jaws.

images.title: 2017 in Paleontology
images.description: This composite paleoart image highlights significant paleontological discoveries and research from 2017, featuring various extinct organisms spanning multiple geological periods and ecosystems.

images.title: Osteolepis panderi
images.description: Osteolepis panderi was a lobe-finned fish from the Paleozoic Era, representing an early member of the Sarcopterygii group that would eventually give rise to tetrapods. This small freshwater fish possessed paired fins with a fleshy lobe at their base, a characteristic feature of sarcopterygians that distinguished them from ray-finned fish.

images.title: Fish and turtles of the Moreno Formation
images.description: The Moreno Formation represents a Late Cretaceous marine ecosystem dominated by diverse fish species and marine turtles inhabiting shallow coastal and shelf environments. This biota reflects the rich biodiversity of the Western Interior Seaway during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages.

images.title: Sulphur Mountain Ichthyopterygians I
images.description: The Sulphur Mountain Formation preserves a diverse assemblage of ichthyopterygians, a group of marine reptiles that dominated Triassic oceans with their streamlined bodies, large eyes, and flipper-like limbs adapted for aquatic hunting. This ecosystem represents a snapshot of early Mesozoic marine life, showcasing the ecological roles these apex predators occupied in ancient seas.

images.title: Hosselkus Limestone
images.description: The Hosselkus Limestone is a Middle Triassic marine fossil deposit from California that preserves a diverse ecosystem of ammonoids, conodonts, and other marine invertebrates. This formation provides crucial insights into Triassic marine communities and their recovery following the Permian-Triassic extinction event.

images.title: Thalattosaurus alexandrae
images.description: Thalattosaurus alexandrae was a marine reptile from the Triassic period belonging to the Thalattosauria, a diverse group of oceangoing sauropterygians. This sleek predator used its powerful tail and flipper-like limbs to hunt fish and other marine organisms in ancient seas.

images.title: Galesaurus planiceps
images.description: Galesaurus planiceps was a small carnivorous therapsid from the Early Triassic of South Africa, representing an early cynodont with advanced mammal-like features. This agile predator played an important role in post-Permian ecosystems as one of the few therapsids to survive the devastating mass extinction event.

images.title: Denwa Formation
images.description: The Denwa Formation is a Middle Permian geological formation in India that preserves a diverse assemblage of early amniotes, synapsids, and other vertebrates from a semi-arid fluvial environment. This ecosystem represents a crucial period in vertebrate evolution during the early dominance of synapsids before the rise of archosaurs.

images.title: Aphaneramma rostratum
images.description: Aphaneramma rostratum is an extinct temnospondyl amphibian from the Carboniferous period, characterized by its distinctive elongated snout and semi-aquatic lifestyle. This small to medium-sized tetrapod was adapted for hunting in freshwater environments during the early evolution of amniotes.

images.title: Cherninia denwai
images.description: Cherninia denwai is an early temnospondyl amphibian from the Carboniferous period, representing a transitional form in the evolution of early tetrapods. As a member of Temnospondyli, it possessed characteristics that bridged aquatic and terrestrial life stages.

images.title: Paracyclotosaurus crookshanki
images.description: Paracyclotosaurus crookshanki was a large temnospondyl amphibian from the Triassic period, characterized by its robust build and powerful jaws adapted for aquatic predation. As a member of the cyclotosaurs, it was one of the dominant semi-aquatic carnivores of its time.

images.title: Basal Cynodonts
images.description: Basal cynodonts were early members of the cynodont lineage that emerged during the Permian period and eventually gave rise to mammals. These small to medium-sized synapsids possessed a mosaic of reptilian and mammalian features, including specialized teeth and skeletal adaptations that foreshadowed the evolution of true mammals.

images.title: Aetosauroides scagliai
images.description: Aetosauroides scagliai was a small aetosaur from the Middle Triassic of South America, characterized by its heavily armored body covered in distinctive bony osteoderms. This herbivorous reptile was an early member of the aetosaur lineage that would diversify significantly during the Late Triassic.

images.title: Sillosuchus longicervix
images.description: Sillosuchus longicervix was a medium-sized poposauroid from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, characterized by its notably elongated neck that distinguished it from other members of its clade. As a predatory archosaur, it occupied an important ecological role in Triassic ecosystems before the eventual dominance of dinosaurs.

images.title: Probainognathus jenseni
images.description: Probainognathus jenseni was a small, early cynodon from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, representing an intermediate stage in the evolution of therapsids toward mammals. This cat-sized predator possessed an advanced jaw structure and teeth arrangement that foreshadowed the specialized dentition of true mammals.

images.title: Shringasaurus indicus
images.description: Shringasaurus indicus was a large herbivorous archosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of India, characterized by prominent horn-like projections on its skull. This early relative of crocodilians and dinosaurs represents an important lineage of reptiles that thrived during the Triassic period.

images.title: Pelorocephalus mendozensis
images.description: Pelorocephalus mendozensis was a temnospondyl amphibian from the Triassic period of Argentina, characterized by its distinctive flattened skull and semi-aquatic lifestyle. This early tetrapod represents an important transitional form in the evolution of amphibians during the early Mesozoic era.

images.title: Thelodonti
images.description: Thelodonti were small, jawless fish covered in tiny tooth-like scales called thelodont scales, representing an early branch of agnathans that thrived during the Paleozoic Era. These filter-feeding or detritus-feeding vertebrates occupied ecological niches in marine and freshwater environments before declining in the Mesozoic.

images.title: Archipelepis turbinata
images.description: Archipelepis turbinata is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its small, rounded body and primitive gill structures. This early vertebrate represents an important stage in the evolution of fish before the emergence of jawed fishes.

images.title: Galeaspida
images.description: Galeaspida were small, armored jawless fish from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by their distinctive bony head shields and flattened bodies adapted for bottom-dwelling in ancient seas. These agnathans represent an early experiment in vertebrate armor and were among the first vertebrates to develop complex cranial structures.

images.title: Acanthodii
images.description: Acanthodii were a diverse group of early jawed fish that thrived from the Silurian through the Permian periods, characterized by their spiny fins and streamlined bodies. Often called 'spiny sharks,' these pioneering vertebrates represent an important evolutionary step between jawless fish and modern sharks, though they were not direct shark ancestors.

images.title: Acanthodes bronni
images.description: Acanthodes bronni is an extinct acanthodian, a spiny-finned fish from the Paleozoic Era characterized by sharp spines supporting its fins. This small predatory fish inhabited freshwater and marine environments during the Carboniferous period.

images.title: Climatius reticulatus
images.description: Climatius reticulatus was a small acanthodian fish from the Early Devonian period, characterized by its heavily spined fins and reticulated (net-like) scale patterns. These early jawed fish were among the first vertebrates to develop a diverse array of fin spines, which likely served in prey capture and defense.

images.title: Ischnacanthus gracilis
images.description: Ischnacanthus gracilis was a small, early acanthodian fish from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its gracile build and prominent spines along its fins. This spiny-finned fish represents an important early group of jawed vertebrates that thrived in ancient marine and freshwater environments.

images.title: Laxaspis qujingensis
images.description: Laxaspis qujingensis is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Silurian period, characterized by its distinctive bony armor plating and flattened body form. This small ostracoderm represents the early diversification of armored fish in ancient marine environments.

images.title: Hanyangaspis guodingshanensis
images.description: Hanyangaspis guodingshanensis is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Silurian period of China, characterized by its distinctive bony head shield and small body size. This primitive vertebrate represents an important evolutionary stage in the development of early fish before the rise of jawed fishes.

images.title: Pisanosaurus mertii
images.description: Pisanosaurus mertii is one of the earliest known dinosauromorphs from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, representing a small, bipedal herbivore that preceded the radiation of true dinosaurs. This genus provides crucial insights into the early evolution of the dinosaur lineage and the transition from archosaurian ancestors to the dinosaurs that would dominate the Mesozoic.

images.title: Parvancorina minchami
images.description: Parvancorina minchami is a small, disc-shaped organism from the Ediacaran period, characterized by its flattened body and radial symmetry. This enigmatic creature remains poorly understood, though it may represent an early form of echinoderm or an entirely extinct body plan from Earth's earliest complex life.

images.title: Aletopelta coombsi
images.description: Aletopelta coombsi was a nodosaur ankylosaur from the Early Cretaceous of North America, characterized by its heavily armored body covered in bony osteoderms. As a member of Thyreophora, it was a herbivorous dinosaur specialized for defense against large predators through its thick armor plating.

images.title: Mauriciosaurus fernandezi
images.description: Mauriciosaurus fernandezi was a medium-sized sauropterygian marine reptile from the Early Cretaceous period. This paddle-limbed predator inhabited shallow marine environments and represents an important transitional form within the sauropterygian lineage.

images.title: Parietobalaena yamaokai
images.description: Parietobalaena yamaokai is an extinct baleen whale from the Miocene epoch that represents an early member of the balaenid family. This cetacean inhabited ancient marine environments and provides insight into the evolution of filter-feeding whales.

images.title: Cranioceras unicornis
images.description: Cranioceras unicornis was a small artiodactyl from the Eocene epoch, characterized by a distinctive single horn-like cranial projection on its forehead. This early even-toed ungulate represents an experimental phase in artiodactyl evolution before the diversification of modern horned and antlered forms.

images.title: New dinosaur phylogeny
images.description: This phylogenetic diagram illustrates the evolutionary relationships and classification of dinosaurs, showing how different dinosaur groups diverged and evolved throughout the Mesozoic Era. Such phylogenies help paleontologists understand the connections between various dinosaur species and their common ancestors.

images.title: Merriamoceros coronatus
images.description: Merriamoceros coronatus was a small, horned artiodactyl from the Eocene epoch, characterized by the distinctive bony protrusions on its head that gave it its 'crowned' name. This early ruminant represents an important stage in the evolution of horned ungulates during the early Cenozoic.

images.title: Opabinia regalis
images.description: Opabinia regalis was a bizarre predatory arthropod from the Middle Cambrian period, notable for its five eyes, flexible trunk-like appendage, and segmented body adapted for hunting in ancient seafloor environments. This unusual creature represents one of the most distinctive members of the Burgess Shale fauna and showcases the remarkable diversity of early arthropod body plans.

images.title: Ottoia prolifica
images.description: Ottoia prolifica is an extinct priapulid (penis worm) from the Cambrian period, characterized by its elongated body with a retractable proboscis armed with hooks used for feeding and burrowing. This small marine worm was a common predator and scavenger in early Paleozoic oceans, particularly abundant in the Burgess Shale fauna.

images.title: Postosuchus kirkpatricki
images.description: Postosuchus kirkpatricki was a large rauisuchian archosaur from the Triassic period, reaching lengths of up to 6 meters. As an apex predator of its time, it was a formidable terrestrial carnivore with a powerful bite and robust build, representing one of the dominant predators before the rise of dinosaurs.

images.title: Anomalocaris saron
images.description: Anomalocaris saron was a large apex predator of the Cambrian seas, reaching lengths of up to 1 meter, with a distinctive circular mouth and grasping front appendages used to capture prey. This iconic arthropod represents one of the most successful hunters of the early Paleozoic and is a key species in understanding the Cambrian explosion of animal diversity.

images.title: Carnotaurus sastrei
images.description: Carnotaurus sastrei was a large theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Argentina, distinguished by prominent horns above its eyes and a powerful build adapted for hunting. This carnivore was one of the largest predators of its time and likely relied on strength and speed to capture prey.

images.title: Eoredlichia intermedia
images.description: Eoredlichia intermedia is an early arthropod from the Cambrian period, representing a transitional form in arthropod evolution. This small marine creature possessed features intermediate between more primitive arthropods and later trilobite-like forms.

images.title: Saccorhytus coronarius
images.description: Saccorhytus coronarius is an early deuterostome from the Cambrian period, representing one of the most primitive known ancestors of vertebrates. This tiny, bag-like organism possessed a distinctive crown of spines around its mouth and represents a crucial link in understanding the evolution of chordate body plans.

images.title: Moropus elatus
images.description: Moropus elatus was a large chalicothere from the Eocene epoch, belonging to an unusual group of perissodactyls that combined features of horses, camels, and claws. These herbivorous mammals used their powerful forelimbs and large claws to pull down vegetation and dig, representing a unique evolutionary experiment in ungulate morphology.

images.title: Stegotetrabelodon syrticus
images.description: Stegotetrabelodon syrticus was a Miocene proboscidean characterized by its distinctive four tusks—two in the upper jaw and two in the lower jaw—which gave the genus its name. This North African elephant relative inhabited savanna and woodland environments during the middle Miocene epoch.

images.title: Hallucigenia sparsa
images.description: Hallucigenia sparsa was a bizarre, worm-like creature from the Cambrian period featuring a row of dorsal spines and tentacle-like appendages used for feeding and locomotion. This onychophoran relative represents one of the most unusual body plans discovered in the famous Burgess Shale fossil beds.

images.title: Prolibytherium magnieri
images.description: Prolibytherium magnieri was an early artiodactyl from the Eocene epoch of North Africa, representing one of the earliest members of the even-toed ungulate lineage. This small, deer-like mammal inhabited the lush forested environments of what is now Libya during a time of warm global climates.

images.title: Brachiosaurus altithorax
images.description: Brachiosaurus altithorax was a massive sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic period, characterized by its notably long front legs that elevated its shoulders higher than its hips—an unusual body plan among sauropods. This herbivorous giant could reach lengths of up to 85 feet and weighed as much as 56 tons, making it one of the largest land animals to have ever existed.

images.title: Merychippus insignis
images.description: Merychippus insignis was a small to medium-sized equid from the Miocene epoch, representing an important transitional form in horse evolution with three-toed feet and grazing adaptations. This genus played a crucial role in the diversification of horses as grasslands expanded across North America.

images.title: Gomphotaria pugnax
images.description: Gomphotaria pugnax was an extinct walrus-like pinniped from the Miocene epoch, characterized by its robust build and specialized tusks used for hauling out on ice and competing with other males. This marine carnivore inhabited cold coastal waters and represents an early branch in pinniped evolution.

images.title: Menoceras barbouri
images.description: Menoceras barbouri was a small, early perissodactyl ungulate from the Oligocene epoch, belonging to the rhinoceros-like family Lophiodontidae. This diminutive mammal represents an important transitional form in the evolution of hoofed mammals during the early Paleogene.

images.title: Zalambdalestes lechei
images.description: Zalambdalestes lechei was a small, shrew-like early mammal from the Early Cretaceous period that possessed specialized teeth adapted for an insectivorous diet. This agile creature represents an important lineage of early mammals that thrived during the age of dinosaurs.

images.title: Thylacosmilus atrox
images.description: Thylacosmilus atrox was a saber-toothed marsupial carnivore from South America during the Pliocene epoch, equipped with elongated canine teeth similar to those of saber-toothed cats. As an apex predator of its time, it hunted large herbivorous mammals in its native environment.

images.title: Plotosaurus bennisovi
images.description: Plotosaurus bennisovi was a large marine mosasaur from the Late Cretaceous period, reaching lengths of up to 13 meters. As an apex predator of shallow seas, it possessed powerful jaws and a paddle-like tail for hunting fish and smaller marine reptiles.

images.title: Wahlisaurus massarae
images.description: Wahlisaurus massarae was a relatively small ichthyosaur from the Middle Triassic period, representing an early member of this successful lineage of marine reptiles. These dolphin-like predators were adapted for life in ancient seas, hunting fish and other marine organisms with their streamlined bodies and powerful flippers.

images.title: Californosaurus perrini
images.description: Californosaurus perrini was a medium-sized ichthyosaur from the Early Jurassic period that inhabited the ancient seas of what is now California. This marine reptile was an efficient predator adapted to oceanic life with its streamlined body and powerful tail for swimming.

images.title: Aepycamelus giraffinus
images.description: Aepycamelus giraffinus was a long-necked camelid from the Miocene epoch, representing one of the tallest members of the camel family and an example of convergent evolution with giraffes. This extinct genus adapted to browsing on high vegetation in North American grasslands and open woodlands.

images.title: Ambulocetus natans
images.description: Ambulocetus natans was an early cetacean from the Eocene epoch that represents a transitional form between land-dwelling mammals and fully aquatic whales. This semi-aquatic predator possessed hind limbs, a long tail, and adaptations for both swimming and terrestrial locomotion.

images.title: Murusraptor barrosaensis
images.description: Murusraptor barrosaensis was a mid-sized dromaeosaurian theropod from Early Cretaceous Argentina, characterized by its agile build and predatory adaptations typical of raptorial dinosaurs. This carnivorous dinosaur represents an important member of South American theropod fauna during the Cretaceous period.

images.title: Quetzalcoatlus northropi
images.description: Quetzalcoatlus northropi was one of the largest flying animals ever to exist, with a wingspan estimated at 10-11 meters and a mass of approximately 200-250 kilograms. This Late Cretaceous pterosaur from North America likely hunted large prey using its long, powerful beak and neck, making it an apex predator of its time.

images.title: Gualicho shinyae
images.description: Gualicho shinyae is a medium-sized theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Argentina, notable for its unusual combination of primitive and derived features. This enigmatic predator represents an important transitional form in theropod evolution during the Cretaceous period.

images.title: Triceratops horridus
images.description: Triceratops horridus was a large ceratopsian dinosaur characterized by its distinctive three-horn facial arrangement and prominent bony frill. This Late Cretaceous herbivore was one of the last dinosaurs to exist before the end-Cretaceous extinction event.

images.title: Arizonasaurus babbitti
images.description: Arizonasaurus babbitti was an early rauisuchian from the Middle Triassic of Arizona, representing one of the apex predators of its time before the rise of dinosaurs. This semi-aquatic reptile possessed a powerful build and was among the dominant carnivores of the Triassic period.

images.title: Palaeolagus haydeni
images.description: Palaeolagus haydeni is an extinct early rabbit from the Eocene epoch, representing one of the most primitive known members of the lagomorph family. This small herbivorous mammal lived in the forests and grasslands of North America and shows transitional characteristics between modern rabbits and their earlier ancestors.

images.title: Tyrannosaurus rex
images.description: Tyrannosaurus rex was a massive bipedal carnivorous theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period, reaching lengths of up to 12 meters and standing as one of the largest terrestrial predators to ever exist. It possessed powerful hind limbs, a strong tail for balance, and a massive skull equipped with sharp teeth adapted for hunting large herbivorous dinosaurs.

images.title: Nanotyrannus lancensis
images.description: Nanotyrannus lancensis was a small tyrannosaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of North America, measuring around 5 meters in length. This agile predator possessed sharp teeth and claws, likely hunting small to medium-sized dinosaurs in its ecosystem.

images.title: Brachychampsa montana
images.description: Brachychampsa montana was a small, short-snouted crocodylomorph that lived during the Paleocene epoch in what is now Montana. This early relative of modern crocodilians was adapted to freshwater environments and represents the crocodylomorph lineage during the early radiation of mammals in the post-dinosaur world.

images.title: Didelphodon vorax
images.description: Didelphodon vorax was a small, carnivorous mammal from the Late Cretaceous that represents one of the largest known mammals of its time. This fierce predator possessed sharp teeth and claws, making it an apex hunter among early mammals despite its modest size.

images.title: Acheroraptor temertyorum
images.description: Acheroraptor temertyorum was a small dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, measuring only about 60 centimeters in length. Despite its diminutive size, it possessed the characteristic curved killing claw and predatory adaptations typical of its raptor family.

images.title: Fukuivenator paradoxus
images.description: Fukuivenator paradoxus was a small theropod dinosaur from Early Cretaceous Japan, notable for its mosaic of primitive and derived features that challenge traditional theropod classification. This unusual dinosaur exhibits a combination of traits that make it difficult to place within standard theropod groups, earning its name 'paradoxus'.

images.title: Eotrachodon orientalis
images.description: Eotrachodon orientalis is an early ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Mongolia, representing a transitional form between basal ornithopods and more derived iguanodonts. This small herbivorous dinosaur exhibits dental and skeletal features that help us understand the evolution of the ornithopod lineage.

images.title: Spiclypeus shipporum
images.description: Spiclypeus shipporum was a small ceratopsian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Montana, characterized by distinctive spike-like projections on its frill. This herbivorous dinosaur represents one of the more unusual members of the Ceratopsia, with unique cranial ornamentation that likely served in species recognition or display.

images.title: Apatoraptor pennatus
images.description: Apatoraptor pennatus is a small dromaeosaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, characterized by its relatively short stature and well-developed feathers. This early raptor represents an intermediate form in the evolution of dromaeosaurs during the mid-Cretaceous period.

images.title: Machairoceratops cronusi
images.description: Machairoceratops cronusi was a small ceratopsian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Utah, notable for its distinctive saber-like horns above the eyes. This early horned dinosaur represents an important transitional form in ceratopsian evolution.

images.title: Ateleaspis tesselata
images.description: Ateleaspis tesselata is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its distinctive tessellated armor plating that covered its head and body. This small, filter-feeding vertebrate represents an early stage in vertebrate evolution before the development of true jaws.

images.title: Cathaymyrus diadexus
images.description: Cathaymyrus diadexus is an early cephalochordate from the Middle Cambrian period, representing a primitive relative of modern lancelets. This small, fish-like creature possessed features intermediate between invertebrates and vertebrates, making it important for understanding chordate evolution.

images.title: Atopodentatus unicus
images.description: Atopodentatus unicus was a bizarre Triassic marine reptile with an unusual shovel-like snout and specialized feeding adaptations, representing one of the most morphologically distinctive sauropterygians. This peculiar creature occupied an ecological niche unlike other known members of its group, making it a fascinating example of reptilian diversity in Mesozoic seas.

images.title: Henodus chelyops
images.description: Henodus chelyops was a small, turtle-like sauropterygian from the Triassic period, characterized by its flattened body and unique eye-like openings in its skull. This pachypleurosaur was a specialized marine reptile adapted for hunting small prey in shallow seas.

images.title: Yunguisaurus liae
images.description: Yunguisaurus liae is an early sauropterygian from the Middle Triassic of China, representing a transitional form in the evolution of marine reptiles. This small, long-necked aquatic reptile demonstrates adaptations for life in shallow marine and brackish water environments.

images.title: Hypsognathus fenneri
images.description: Hypsognathus fenneri was a small procolophonomorph reptile from the Early Triassic period, characterized by its robust skull and specialized teeth adapted for crushing hard-bodied prey. This early amniote represents an important lineage of small reptiles that survived the Permian-Triassic extinction event.

images.title: Hyperokynodon keuperinus
images.description: Hyperokynodon keuperinus was a large temnospondyl amphibian from the Triassic period, characterized by robust jaws and powerful teeth adapted for predation. This semi-aquatic creature inhabited freshwater environments and represents the diverse radiation of temnospondyls during the Mesozoic era.

images.title: Eudimorphodon ranzii
images.description: Eudimorphodon ranzii was an early pterosaur from the Triassic period, notable for possessing two distinctly different types of teeth—a primitive characteristic among flying reptiles. This small, insectivorous pterosaur represents an important transitional form in pterosaur evolution.

images.title: Dimorphodon macronyx
images.description: Dimorphodon macronyx was an early pterosaur from the Early Jurassic period, characterized by its distinctive large head, sharp teeth, and powerful clawed feet. Despite its fearsome appearance, it was likely an insectivore or piscivore adapted to coastal and semi-aquatic environments.

images.title: Mayomyzon pieckoensis
images.description: Mayomyzon pieckoensis is an extinct jawless fish (agnathan) from the Carboniferous period, representing an early relative of modern lampreys and hagfishes. This small, eel-like creature possessed a toothed sucking disc and inhabited freshwater environments millions of years before the evolution of jawed vertebrates.

images.title: Eodromaeus murphi
images.description: Eodromaeus murphi is an early theropod dinosaur from the Triassic period of Argentina, representing one of the most basal members of the theropod lineage. This small, bipedal predator exhibits primitive characteristics and provides crucial insights into the early evolution of theropod dinosaurs.

images.title: Steneosaurus bollensis
images.description: Steneosaurus bollensis was a small to medium-sized crocodylomorph from the Early Jurassic period, known from fossils found in Germany. This marine crocodilian was adapted for life in shallow seas and coastal environments of the Jurassic.

images.title: Pipiscius zangerli
images.description: Pipiscius zangerli is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Silurian period, characterized by its small size and primitive fin structures. This ancient vertebrate represents an early stage in fish evolution before the development of jaws.

images.title: Gilpichthys greenei
images.description: Gilpichthys greenei is an extinct agnathan (jawless fish) from the Paleozoic Era, representing an early lineage of vertebrates that lacked jaws and paired fins. This primitive fish was part of the diverse assemblages of early vertebrates that inhabited ancient marine and freshwater environments.

images.title: Tullimonstrum gregarium
images.description: Tullimonstrum gregarium, commonly known as the Tully monster, was a small soft-bodied animal from the Carboniferous period whose distinctive elongated body, tooth-studded proboscis, and fins made it one of the most enigmatic creatures in the fossil record. Long considered a unique and unclassifiable organism, it has recently been reinterpreted as an early jawless fish (agnathan) related to lampreys.

images.title: Wumengosaurus delicatomandibularis
images.description: Wumengosaurus delicatomandibularis is an early sauropterygian from the Middle Triassic of China, notable for its gracile mandible and relatively small size compared to later marine reptiles. This basal member of Sauropterygia represents an important transitional form in the evolution of marine-adapted reptiles.

images.title: Keichousaurus hui
images.description: Keichousaurus hui was a small marine reptile from the Triassic period, belonging to the sauropterygians, a diverse group of aquatic predators. It possessed a long neck, streamlined body, and paddle-like limbs adapted for life in ancient seas.

images.title: Cotylorhynchus romeri
images.description: Cotylorhynchus romeri was a large herbivorous pelycosaur from the Early Permian period, characterized by its robust build and distinctive dental adaptations for processing tough plant material. As one of the largest synapsids of its time, it represents an important early experiment in mammal-like reptile evolution.

images.title: Eothyris parkeri
images.description: Eothyris parkeri was an early synapsid from the Carboniferous period, representing one of the primitive pelycosaurs that preceded the later mammal-like reptiles. This small, lizard-like creature was an important early member of the synapsid lineage that would eventually lead to mammals.

images.title: Varanops brevirostris
images.description: Varanops brevirostris was a small carnivorous pelycosaur from the Early Permian period, characterized by its short snout and sharp teeth adapted for hunting small vertebrates. As one of the early synapsids, it represents an important lineage in the evolution toward modern mammals.

images.title: Mycterosaurus longiceps
images.description: Mycterosaurus longiceps was a small carnivorous pelycosaur from the Early Permian period, characterized by its notably elongated skull and primitive synapsid anatomy. As an early member of the synapsid lineage, it represents an important evolutionary step toward modern mammals.

images.title: Dracoraptor hanigani
images.description: Dracoraptor hanigani is an early theropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic period of Wales, representing one of the most primitive known members of the dromaeosaur lineage. This small predator possessed a blend of primitive and derived features, including a notably large claw on its second toe and relatively short arms.

images.title: Argentavis magnificens
images.description: Argentavis magnificens was a massive teratornis from South America during the Miocene epoch, with a wingspan estimated between 6-7 meters, making it one of the largest flying birds ever to exist. This powerful predator likely soared over open grasslands and woodlands, hunting large mammals and smaller vertebrates.

images.title: Notocolossus gonzalezparejasi
images.description: Notocolossus gonzalezparejasi was a massive sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of South America, representing one of the largest land animals to have ever existed. This colossal herbivore possessed an extremely long neck and tail, which it used to reach high vegetation and maintain balance.

images.title: Onychonycteris finneyi
images.description: Onychonycteris finneyi is an early bat from the early Eocene epoch, representing one of the most primitive known members of Chiroptera with claws on its wings. This transitional fossil provides crucial insights into the evolution of flight and echolocation in bats.

images.title: Platybelodon grangeri
images.description: Platybelodon grangeri was a large proboscidean from the Miocene epoch, characterized by its distinctive flattened, shovel-like lower tusks that it likely used for digging and stripping vegetation. This bizarre elephant relative represents an experimental branch of tusk evolution that ultimately proved unsuccessful and went extinct.

images.title: Eomanis waldi
images.description: Eomanis waldi is one of the earliest known pangolins, representing a transitional form in the evolution of Pholidota during the Eocene epoch. This small, scaly mammal exemplifies the ancient origins of the pangolin lineage, which would eventually diversify into the modern pangolin species we see today.

images.title: Deinogalerix koenigswaldi
images.description: Deinogalerix koenigswaldi was a giant hedgehog-like eulipotyphlan from the Miocene epoch, reaching sizes much larger than modern hedgehogs at up to 60 centimeters in length. This insectivorous mammal inhabited the islands of the Mediterranean region and likely preyed on invertebrates and small vertebrates.

images.title: Seismosaurus halli
images.description: Seismosaurus halli was one of the longest sauropods ever discovered, a massive herbivorous dinosaur that reached lengths of over 100 feet and weighed up to 80 tons. This Late Jurassic giant roamed North America using its extremely long neck to browse vegetation from high canopy levels that other herbivores could not reach.

images.title: Amargasaurus cazaui
images.description: Amargasaurus cazaui was a Early Cretaceous sauropod from Argentina notable for its unusual paired rows of tall neural spines along its neck and back, which may have supported a sail-like structure or served defensive purposes. This medium-sized sauropod represents a unique adaptation among long-necked dinosaurs and provides insight into sauropod diversity during the Early Cretaceous period.

images.title: Helicoprion bessonovi
images.description: Helicoprion bessonovi was a bizarre chimaera-like shark from the Permian period, characterized by a distinctive spiral tooth whorl on its lower jaw that it likely used for crushing hard-bodied prey. This unusual feeding apparatus represents one of the most specialized dentitions among prehistoric chondrichthyans.

images.title: Tupandactylus imperator
images.description: Tupandactylus imperator was a large pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous period, characterized by an impressive cranial crest and a wingspan estimated at around 4-5 meters. This flying reptile was one of the most distinctive members of the Anhanguera family, known for its impressive head ornamentation.

images.title: Albertosaurus sarcophagus
images.description: Albertosaurus sarcophagus was a mid-sized theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of North America, measuring around 8-9 meters in length. As an apex predator of its time, it likely hunted large herbivorous dinosaurs and was known for its powerful bite and sharp teeth.

images.title: Incisivosaurus gauthieri
images.description: Incisivosaurus gauthieri was an early troodontid theropod from the Early Cretaceous of China, notable for its unusual prominent incisor-like teeth adapted for an omnivorous diet. This small, feathered dinosaur represents a transitional form in the evolution of these intelligent predators.

images.title: Kosmoceratops richardsoni
images.description: Kosmoceratops richardsoni was a horned ceratopsian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Utah, notable for its elaborate array of horns and frills, featuring an unusual arrangement of cranial ornamentation among ceratopsians. This medium-sized herbivore represents the diverse radiation of ceratopsian dinosaurs in North America during the late Mesozoic era.

images.title: Xenacanthus decheni
images.description: Xenacanthus decheni was a small freshwater shark belonging to the extinct group of strap-toothed sharks (xenacanthids) that inhabited Paleozoic waters. These primitive sharks were characterized by their elongated bodies, fin spines, and specialized tooth arrangements adapted for capturing small prey in ancient freshwater ecosystems.

images.title: Cladoselache fyleri
images.description: Cladoselache fyleri was an early shark from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its streamlined body, paired fins, and primitive jaw structure. As one of the oldest known sharks, it represents an important transitional form in the evolution of cartilaginous fishes.

images.title: Lungmenshanaspis kiangyouensis
images.description: Lungmenshanaspis kiangyouensis is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Silurian period of China, belonging to the heterostracans. This armored fish represents an early lineage of ostracoderms that preceded the evolution of true jaws in vertebrates.

images.title: Zenaspis pagei
images.description: Zenaspis pagei was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Devonian period, characterized by its flattened body and bony head shield. This small fish inhabited ancient freshwater and marine environments during the early diversification of vertebrates.

images.title: Lasanius problematicus
images.description: Lasanius problematicus is an enigmatic agnathan from the Ordovician period whose taxonomic classification remains uncertain. This early jawless fish represents one of the problematic fossil forms that helps illuminate the early evolution of vertebrates.

images.title: Hurdia victoria
images.description: Hurdia victoria was a large radiodontan arthropod from the Middle Cambrian period, characterized by its distinctive head appendages and formidable predatory adaptations. This apex predator of ancient seas possessed powerful raptorial claws and likely fed on other arthropods and small organisms in early marine ecosystems.

images.title: Thelodus parvidens
images.description: Thelodus parvidens was a small, jawless fish from the Paleozoic Era, belonging to the thelodonts, an early group of agnathans with heavily armored bodies covered in microscopic placoid scales. These primitive vertebrates were among the earliest fish to inhabit ancient seas and freshwater environments.

images.title: Didazoon haoae
images.description: Didazoon haoae is an extinct vetulicolian from the early Cambrian period, representing a bizarre group of filter-feeding marine animals with an elongated body and distinctive gill structures. This small, soft-bodied organism inhabited ancient seas and provides insight into the early diversification of deuterostome lineages during the Cambrian explosion.

images.title: Waptia fieldensis
images.description: Waptia fieldensis was a small arthropod from the Middle Cambrian Burgess Shale, characterized by its elongated body, paired appendages, and protective dorsal carapace. This creature represents an early form of arthropod complexity during the Cambrian explosion of life.

images.title: Nectocaris pteryx
images.description: Nectocaris pteryx was a small, soft-bodied cephalopod-like mollusc from the Middle Cambrian period, characterized by its distinctive wing-like appendages and streamlined body adapted for swimming. This early cephalopod ancestor represents an important evolutionary step in the diversification of molluscs during the Cambrian explosion.

images.title: Tribrachidium heraldicum
images.description: Tribrachidium heraldicum is a small, disc-shaped organism from the Ediacaran fauna characterized by three-fold radial symmetry and a distinctive tri-lobed body plan. This mysterious creature remains one of the most enigmatic members of the Ediacaran biota, with its ecological role and phylogenetic affinities still debated among paleontologists.

images.title: Myxinikela siroka
images.description: Myxinikela siroka is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Cambrian period, representing a primitive vertebrate with a simple body plan. This small, eel-like creature is known from the Burgess Shale and represents an early stage in vertebrate evolution before the development of jaws.

images.title: Hibernaspis macrolepis
images.description: Hibernaspis macrolepis was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Silurian period, characterized by its large scales and armored head region typical of early vertebrates. This small, bottom-dwelling creature represents an important stage in vertebrate evolution before the rise of jawed fishes.

images.title: Gabreyaspis tarda
images.description: Gabreyaspis tarda is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its armored head shield and primitive body structure. This early vertebrate represents a crucial stage in the evolution of fish before the development of jaws.

images.title: Pycnosteus tuberculatus
images.description: Pycnosteus tuberculatus is an extinct agnathan (jawless fish) from the Devonian period, characterized by its heavily armored head and body covered in bony tubercles. This ostracoderm represents an early stage in vertebrate evolution before the development of true jaws.

images.title: Anomalocaris canadensis
images.description: Anomalocaris canadensis was a large predatory arthropod from the Middle Cambrian period, reaching lengths of up to one meter, with a distinctive circular mouth and grasping frontal appendages used to capture prey. It was one of the dominant apex predators of the Burgess Shale ecosystem and represents an early experiment in large-bodied animal predation.

images.title: Psammolepis venyukovi
images.description: Psammolepis venyukovi was an early acanthodian, a small armored jawless fish from the Paleozoic Era. This ancient agnathan was characterized by its flattened body and elaborate bony plates, representing an important early stage in vertebrate evolution.

images.title: Hemicyclaspis murchisoni
images.description: Hemicyclaspis murchisoni was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Devonian period, characterized by its distinctive semicircular head shield and flattened body adapted for bottom-dwelling in ancient seas. This ostracoderm represents an important stage in vertebrate evolution before the rise of jawed fishes.

images.title: Phlebolepis elegans
images.description: Phlebolepis elegans was an early agnathan (jawless fish) from the Devonian period, characterized by its small, elongated body and distinctive scale-like placoid structures covering its skin. This primitive fish represents an important stage in vertebrate evolution, existing before the development of true jaws and paired fins.

images.title: Anglaspis heintzi
images.description: Anglaspis heintzi was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its heavily armored head shield and small body size. This primitive vertebrate represents an early stage in fish evolution before the development of jaws.

images.title: Pikaia gracilens
images.description: Pikaia gracilens is an early chordate from the Middle Cambrian period, known from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia. This small, eel-like creature possessed a notochord and is considered one of the earliest known ancestors of all vertebrates.

images.title: Tawa hallae
images.description: Tawa hallae is an early theropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic period of North America, representing a primitive member of the theropod lineage that would eventually lead to T. rex and modern birds. This bipedal predator was relatively small, measuring around 2 meters in length, and possessed features that bridge earlier dinosaurs with more derived theropods.

images.title: Clydagnathus cavusformis
images.description: Clydagnathus cavusformis is an extinct conodont, a small agnathan vertebrate known primarily from its distinctive tooth-like phosphatic elements called conodont elements. These microscopic organisms were abundant in marine environments during the Paleozoic Era and are valuable index fossils for biostratigraphy.

images.title: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis
images.description: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis was an early theropod dinosaur from the Late Triassic period, representing one of the oldest known members of Theropoda. This bipedal carnivore ranged from 3.5 to 6 meters in length and exhibited a mosaic of primitive and derived characteristics, making it a crucial link in understanding dinosaur evolution.

images.title: Eoraptor lunensis
images.description: Eoraptor lunensis was one of the earliest known theropod dinosaurs, a small bipedal carnivore from the Early Triassic period of Argentina. Despite being classified as a sauropodomorph relative, it represents a transitional form showing characteristics of both early theropods and sauropodomorph lineages.

images.title: Lagerpeton chanarensis
images.description: Lagerpeton chanarensis was a small, bipedal dinosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, representing an early relative of dinosaurs. This fox-sized creature possessed long hindlimbs and a long tail, suggesting an agile, cursorial lifestyle that predated the rise of true dinosaurs.

images.title: Saltopus elginensis
images.description: Saltopus elginensis was a tiny dinosauromorph from the Early Triassic of Scotland, measuring only about 24-39 centimeters in length. This diminutive creature represents some of the earliest known members of the lineage leading to dinosaurs, with a lightweight build adapted for agile movement.

images.title: Marasuchus lilloensis
images.description: Marasuchus lilloensis was a small, early dinosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, representing a transitional form between dinosaurs and their non-dinosaurian archosaurian ancestors. This bipedal reptile possessed characteristics that would become hallmarks of dinosaurs, including an upright posture and specialized hip structure.

images.title: Lewisuchus admixtus
images.description: Lewisuchus admixtus was an early dinosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of Argentina, representing a small, bipedal predator that shared characteristics with both dinosaurs and their close relatives. As a transitional form, it provides important insights into the evolutionary lineage leading to true dinosaurs.

images.title: Sacisaurus agudoensis
images.description: Sacisaurus agudoensis is an early dinosauromorph from the Middle Triassic of Brazil, representing a transitional form between non-dinosaurian dinosauromorphs and true dinosaurs. This small, bipedal reptile exhibits characteristics that help us understand the early evolution of the dinosaurian lineage.

images.title: Trilophosaurus buettneri
images.description: Trilophosaurus buettneri was a small, herbivorous reptile from the Triassic period, characterized by three prominent ridges along its skull that gave the genus its distinctive name. This early synapsid-related reptile was an early experiment in herbivory during the Triassic ecosystem.

images.title: Simolestes vorax
images.description: Simolestes vorax was a large marine reptile belonging to the Sauropterygia, an extinct group of carnivorous aquatic reptiles that dominated Mesozoic oceans. This fierce predator possessed powerful jaws and flippers, making it an apex hunter in the shallow seas of the Jurassic period.

images.title: Cryptoclidus eurymerus
images.description: Cryptoclidus eurymerus was a plesiosaur from the Middle Jurassic period, characterized by its long neck, small head, and four paddle-like limbs adapted for marine locomotion. This sauropterygian was a successful marine predator that hunted fish and other small aquatic prey in shallow seas.

images.title: Brachypterygius extremus
images.description: Brachypterygius extremus was a relatively small ichthyosaur from the Early Cretaceous period, characterized by its short flippers and streamlined body adapted for marine hunting. This member of Ichthyosauria represents the later diversity of these successful marine reptiles before their extinction.

images.title: Tremataspis mammillata
images.description: Tremataspis mammillata is an early agnathan (jawless fish) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its distinctive bony armor plating and small size. This primitive vertebrate represents an important stage in early fish evolution, before the development of jaws.

images.title: Bothriolepis canadensis
images.description: Bothriolepis canadensis is an antiarch placoderm from the Devonian period, characterized by its heavily armored head and thorax with bony plates and jointed pectoral appendages. This freshwater fish was one of the most successful armored fishes of its time, possessing a small mouth adapted for bottom-feeding and filter-feeding behaviors.

images.title: Drepanaspis gemuendenensis
images.description: Drepanaspis gemuendenensis was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Devonian period, characterized by its distinctive flattened body and curved tooth-like structures used for feeding on the seafloor. This small armored fish inhabited shallow marine environments and represents an important transitional form in early vertebrate evolution.

images.title: Mesomyzon mengae
images.description: Mesomyzon mengae is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Cambrian period, known from fossils in China. It represents an important early stage in vertebrate evolution, displaying primitive features of early fish before the development of jaws.

images.title: Kannemeyeria simocephalus
images.description: Kannemeyeria simocephalus was a large herbivorous dicynodont therapsid from the Triassic period, characterized by its massive barrel-shaped body and reduced dentition adapted for plant-eating. This sprawling quadrupedal animal was one of the most successful herbivores of its time, dominating terrestrial ecosystems before the rise of dinosaurs.

images.title: Priscomyzon riniensis
images.description: Priscomyzon riniensis is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Devonian period that represents an intermediate stage in vertebrate evolution. This petromyzontid-like creature possessed the characteristic features of primitive lampreys, including a circular mouth and a notochord-based body plan.

images.title: Pituriaspis doylei
images.description: Pituriaspis doylei was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its small size and primitive armor-like plating. This armored vertebrate represents an important early stage in the evolution of fish before the development of true jaws.

images.title: Yi qi
images.description: Yi qi is a small, bizarre theropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of China, notable for its unusual bat-like wings supported by a greatly elongated fourth finger and membrane rather than feathered wings like other theropods. This unique wing structure represents an independent evolution of flight among dinosaurs and provides insight into the diversity of locomotor strategies in Mesozoic ecosystems.

images.title: Euparkeria capensis
images.description: Euparkeria capensis was a small, agile archosauriform from Early Triassic South Africa, representing an early relative of crocodilians and dinosaurs. This carnivorous reptile was approximately 60 centimeters long and is considered a key transitional form in archosaur evolution.

images.title: Chilesaurus diegosuarezi
images.description: Chilesaurus diegosuarezi is a small theropod dinosaur from Late Jurassic Chile that exhibits unusual mosaic characteristics, combining features typically associated with different dinosaurian lineages. This enigmatic predator represents a unique evolutionary experiment in South American dinosaur fauna.

images.title: Tauraspis rara
images.description: Tauraspis rara is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Ordovician period, characterized by its distinctive armored head shield and small body size. This primitive vertebrate represents an important stage in the early evolution of fish during the Paleozoic Era.

images.title: Furcacauda heintzae
images.description: Furcacauda heintzae is an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its forked tail fin and small, primitive body structure. As a member of the Agnatha, it represents one of the earliest vertebrates to inhabit ancient oceans before the evolution of jaws.

images.title: Cynognathus crateronotus
images.description: Cynognathus crateronotus was a large carnivorous therapsid from the Early Triassic that possessed advanced mammal-like features including differentiated teeth and sophisticated jaw mechanics. This apex predator dominated terrestrial ecosystems in the aftermath of the Permian-Triassic extinction event.

images.title: Erythrosuchus africanus
images.description: Erythrosuchus africanus was a large carnivorous archosauriform from Early Triassic South Africa, representing one of the apex predators of its time with a robust build and powerful jaws. This reptile is considered an important early relative of crocodiles and dinosaurs, helping us understand the early evolution of archosaurs.

images.title: Brontosaurus excelsus
images.description: Brontosaurus excelsus was a massive sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Late Jurassic period, characterized by its enormous long neck, pillar-like legs, and whip-like tail that could reach lengths of up to 72 meters. Despite being previously considered synonymous with Apatosaurus, Brontosaurus was recognized as a distinct genus in 2015 based on anatomical differences in the vertebrae and skeletal structure.

images.title: Hypselosaurus priscus
images.description: Hypselosaurus priscus was a titanosaurian sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of Europe, representing one of the last sauropods to exist before the K-Pg extinction event. This massive herbivore was characterized by its long neck, columnar legs, and relatively small head, typical of the titanosaur group.

images.title: Gyracanthus formosus
images.description: Gyracanthus formosus was a small acanthodian fish from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its streamlined body and prominent spines. As a member of the Acanthodii class, it represents an early group of jawed fishes that thrived in ancient marine and freshwater environments.

images.title: Yawunik kootenayi
images.description: Yawunik kootenayi is a middle Cambrian arthropod from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, characterized by its elongated body and prominent appendages. This marine creature represents the diverse array of early arthropods that dominated Paleozoic oceans.

images.title: Gemuendina stuerzi
images.description: Gemuendina stuerzi was a small, flattened placoderm from the Early Devonian period, characterized by its disc-like body and primitive jaw structures. This early jawed fish represents an important stage in vertebrate evolution, bridging the gap between jawless and modern jawed fish.

images.title: Cephalaspis lyelli
images.description: Cephalaspis lyelli was an early jawless fish (agnathan) from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by a distinctive bony head shield and small size. This filter-feeding animal inhabited freshwater environments during the Silurian and Devonian periods.

images.title: Tiktaalik roseae
images.description: Tiktaalik roseae is a transitional fossil from the Late Devonian period that exhibits characteristics between fish and tetrapods, featuring limb-like fins and a crocodile-like head. This semi-aquatic predator represents a crucial evolutionary link in the fish-to-tetrapod transition and demonstrates how vertebrates first adapted to life on land.

images.title: Psephophorus terrypratchetti
images.description: Psephophorus terrypratchetti is an extinct sea turtle from the Eocene epoch, characterized by its distinctive shell morphology and mosaic-like shell plates. This marine reptile represents an important lineage in the evolutionary history of sea turtles during the early Cenozoic era.

images.title: Koshisaurus katsuyama
images.description: Koshisaurus katsuyama is an early ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Japan, representing a relatively small, bipedal herbivore that lived during the Aptian stage. This genus is significant for its fossil record in the Japanese islands and its role in understanding the early evolution and distribution of ornithopod dinosaurs in East Asia.

images.title: Ctenaspis dentata
images.description: Ctenaspis dentata is an early agnathan (jawless fish) from the Paleozoic Era, characterized by its distinctive tooth-like structures along its body. This primitive vertebrate represents an important stage in the evolution of early fish before the development of jaws.

images.title: Ichthyosaurus anningae
